examples.m: uwepeker anak sunke hawe ka somo ne
examples.place: 大須賀るえ子 (Osuka Rieko), Shiraoi; アイヌ語ラジオ講座テキスト 10
examples.note: A metalinguistic comment on genre: the speaker denies that uwepeker belongs with sunke itak ('lying/false talk'). The predicate hawe ka somo ne ('is also not talk [of that kind]') frames the negation over the noun phrase sunke hawe. hawe = voice/word/talk.

examples.m: pananpe an penanpe an hine sir-an pe ne ru-we ne hike
examples.note: Standard Pananpe–Penanpe opening. The third-person existential frame (no fourth-person a= prefix) contrasts with the first-person fourth-person narration of human prose tales. Hirosawa cites the underlying Tamura audio materials; ruwe ne predicates the simultaneous existence of the two characters as established narrative fact.

examples.m: a=ne ruwe ne sekor amameponcikappo isoytak
examples.place: 川上まつ子 (Kawakami Matsuko), uwepeker '民話15' (ILCAA Ainu materials 022:109)
examples.note: Canonical closing formula. The fourth-person copula a=ne (narrator-as-protagonist 'I am') is wrapped in the quotative sekor, and the verb of narration isoytak then names the fourth-person protagonist amameponcikappo ('Little Sparrow'), disclosing the identity of the first-person narrator. ruwe ne predicates the whole disclosure as established fact.

examples.place: 川上まつ子 (Kawakamimatsuko), ILCAA Ainu materials (AA研アイヌ語資料)
examples.note: Fragment from a human prose tale. The fourth-person prefix a= marks both the possessive relation ('my child') and the transitive subject ('I gave'). Everyday first-person narration would require ku= for both roles; the prose-tale convention substitutes a= throughout.

examples.place: 鍋澤ねぷき (Nabezawa Nepuki), 平取町アイヌ口承文芸, 'カムイユカㇻ ハンチキキ（スズメの酒盛り）'
examples.note: The sakehe hancikiki is the fixed refrain for this sparrow-sake-party kamuy yukar. It precedes the narrative phrase sake-he ci=kar 'we brewed sake'; here sake-he uses the possessed form of sake as an ordinary noun ('the sake'), homophonous with the genre term sakehe 'refrain'. The first-person ci= (1PL.EXCL) marks the deity/group of characters.
Everyday Saru/Chitose: 1SG subject on the singular suppletive stem ek.

Verse register (atomte-itak): the fourth-person intransitive suffix =an appears with the singular stem ek. In prose =an is restricted to plural stems (arki=an 'we come.PL'); the singular + =an combination is a diagnostic of the verse register (Satō 2008: 263).
Everyday (yayan-itak): the locative goal is marked by the free particle ta.

examples.m: kamuy menoko uni-hi tane anakne a=ko-sirepa na
examples.note: Verse register (atomte-itak): the goal is marked by the applicative prefix ko- on the verb, in place of a particle. The fourth-person a= indexes the hero-narrator. This is Satō's illustrative contrast ex. 20.
Constructed to illustrate the 1SG prefix in prayer speech; the ruwe tapan na frame marks formal/ceremonial assertion — see §ruwe-tapan below.

examples.m: tu ray onkami re ray onkami
examples.place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その1)」[aa-irc/006#164]
examples.note: The fourth-person a= is zero-marked here (null allomorph in narrative prose). The numeral-adverb frame tu…re… ('twice…thrice…') with ray (intensifier) is the standard formulaic expression of repeated ritual action. Contrast the 1SG ku= in prayer proper (§person-marking).

examples.m: kamuy menoko uni-hi tane anakne a=ko-sirepa na
examples.note: Satō 2008 ex. 20 (Chitose): elegant-register example contrasting with the colloquial particle-marked form. The goal applicative ko- incorporates the locative relation that would be marked by ta in everyday speech. Here the fourth-person a= marks the (narrative) first person, illustrating the register's applicative morphology in a verse context; in prayer proper, ku- would replace a= (see §person-marking).

examples.m: ko-onkami a ko-onkami a ayne ora
examples.place: 川上まつ子, AA研「uwepeker 民話8(その2)」[aa-irc/007#276]
examples.note: The goal applicative ko- marks the deity as the target of worship; the fourth-person a= indexes the narrative protagonist. The verb reduplication (ko-onkami a ko-onkami a) is the standard iterative-intensive frame in ritual narrative, paralleling the 'twice and three times' pattern in §person-marking.

examples.m: sonno yayrayke kewtum ku=kor wa ku=onkami ru-we tapan na
examples.note: The source text has ku=onkamuy, a form with final -y not found in Saru/Chitose documentation of onkami; it may reflect Samani dialect phonology or a different stem shape. Morphemic line normalised to onkami; the ain line gives the source form. ruwe tapan na is the ceremonial assertion frame.

Polar question via bare ruwe (without ne). The argument of an is zero-marked (3rd person, the sister inside the house). The same formula with an explicit 2SG.S prefix appears later in the same exchange (see §3 below).
o is a non-lexical interjection (Japanese sā 'well then' equivalent). ya in ASA functions as the imperative softener yan of other dialects; the footnote in the source makes this explicit.

e= is the 2SG.S prefix (intransitive subject), marking the addressee as the sole argument of an. totekno (in good health, well) is an adverb modifying the predicate. The polar-question ruwe frame is the same as in §2.

ku= is the 1SG.S prefix, mirroring the 2SG.S e= of the question. The clause-linking particle wa (CONJ) closes the turn without a following clause; in conversational Ainu, a wa-final utterance signals a complete turn while leaving the chain formally open (see Nakagawa 2024: 345).

examples.m: numan poronno upas as kusu tanto sonno merayke na
examples.note: The causal clause (numan … kusu) provides the reason; the main clause (tanto … na) asserts the result. as 'stand/fall' is the standard verb for snowfall (upas as = snow falls). The sentence-final particle na is a soft assertion marker.

merayke=an: the 4th-person intransitive suffix =an attaches to the property verb, yielding a general-experiencer reading ('it is cold out'). Compare merayke na above, where the subject is 3rd-person zero-marked.

nankor encodes inference-based assertion (INFR): the speaker has no direct evidence about tomorrow's weather and reasons from current conditions. The Katakana ナンコンナー represents the ASA sandhi form nankor + na → nankornā.
SA teeta 'here' carries the phonemic long vowel ee; the Saru cognate locative is ta (short). 'an is the singular existential; the suppletive plural form 'okay appears in (2).

'okay is the suppletive plural existential (singular 'an). kaa is the position noun 'above (in contact)' in the elderly register, taking the locative suffix -ta. SA enforces strict grammatical number agreement; the singular 'an would be ungrammatical with a plural subject here.

SA analytic negation: the focus particle ka is followed by the negative predicate hannehka (< han- NEG + copula root), with the copula nee optionally omitted. Hokkaido Saru uses somo ne (NEG COP) instead, an entirely distinct form.

'ariki is the suppletive plural stem of 'come' (singular 'eh); =hci is the SA third-person plural subject suffix cliticized to the verb. HK uses the cognate suppletive plural stem arki, but has no suffix cognate to =hci in this position.

'en= is the SA first-person singular object prefix (1SG.O), cognate with HK en=. The verb yuukara 'recite oral literature' is the SA cognate of HK yukar; the long initial vowel yuu- in SA corresponds to the short yu- of the HK form, consistent with the SA length–accent correspondence discussed in the preceding section.

Illustrating the three boundary symbols: = separates the person marker ku= from the stem (an orthographic convention, not a clitic analysis); - separates the verb root ray from the CAUS suffix. The portmanteau gloss 1SG.A joins two atoms with the dot, expressing person (1SG) and role (A) from a single morpheme.
